definitions.definition: if the conditions stay the same; if other conditions are the same
examples: All things being equal, we should finish the job tomorrow.
All other things being equal, the bigger fighter should win.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: having the same advantages and disadvantages as somebody else
examples: Can our industry compete on equal terms with its overseas rivals?

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: although the members of a society, group, etc. appear to be equal, some, in fact, get better treatment than othersWord Origin
examples: late Middle English: from Latin aequalis, from aequus ‘even, level, equal’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the same in size, quantity, value, etc. as something else
examples: There is an equal number of boys and girls in the class.
Each side will put in an equal amount of money.
Cut it into four equal parts.
The two countries are roughly equal in size.
One unit of alcohol is equal to half a pint of beer.
An area of forest equal to the size of Wales has been destroyed.
legislation to put Gaelic on an equal footing with English
The decision has attracted both praise and criticism in equal measure (= to the same degree).

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: having the same rights or being treated the same as other people, without differences such as race, religion or sex being considered
examples: I believe everyone is born equal.
a society where women and men are equal partners

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: giving people the same rights and opportunities, without differences such as race, religion or sex being considered
examples: equal rights/pay
The company has an equal opportunities policy (= gives the same chances of employment to everyone).
the desire for a more equal society (= in which everyone has the same rights and chances)
The US constitution guarantees equal protection under the law.
The charity's mission is to help provide equal access to education.
the principles of equal treatment and non-discrimination

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: having the necessary strength, courage and ability to deal with something successfully
examples: I hope that he proves equal to the challenge.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: if the conditions stay the same; if other conditions are the same
examples: All things being equal, we should finish the job tomorrow.
All other things being equal, the bigger fighter should win.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: having the same advantages and disadvantages as somebody else
examples: Can our industry compete on equal terms with its overseas rivals?

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: although the members of a society, group, etc. appear to be equal, some, in fact, get better treatment than othersWord Origin
examples: late Middle English: from Latin aequalis, from aequus ‘even, level, equal’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the fact of being equal in rights, status, advantages, etc.
examples: OPPOSITE inequality
racial/social/gender equality
We need to ensure equality of opportunity in all areas of work.
the principle of equality before the law (= the law treats everyone the same)
Don't you believe in equality between men and women?

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to the same degree; in the same or in a similar way
examples: Diet and exercise are equally important.
equally good/impressive/effective
This job could be done equally well by a computer.
Everyone should be treated equally.
The findings of the survey apply equally to adults and children.
The birds are equally at home in a woodland or riverside environment.
She may have arrived late or it is equally possible that she never went there at all.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: in equal parts, amounts, etc.
examples: The money was divided equally among her four children.
They share the housework equally.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: used to introduce another phrase or idea that adds to and is as important as what you have just said
examples: I'm trying to do what is best, but equally I've got to consider the cost.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a statement showing that two amounts or values are equal, for example 2x + y = 54
examples: SEE ALSO differential equation
the numbers on the right-hand side of the equation
the equation for a straight line

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the act of making something equal or considering something as equal (= of equating them)
examples: The equation of wealth with happiness can be dangerous.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a problem or situation in which several things must be considered and dealt with
examples: When children enter the equation, further tensions may arise within a marriage.
Money also comes into the equation.
The availability of public transport is also part of the equation.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to provide yourself/somebody/something with the things that are needed for a particular purpose or activity
examples: SYNONYM kit out/up
to be fully/poorly equipped
She got a bank loan to rent and equip a small workshop.
He equipped himself with a street plan.
The centre is well equipped for canoeing and mountaineering.
Rooms vary in size and come equipped with hairdryers, television and telephone.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to prepare somebody for an activity or task, especially by teaching them what they need to know
examples: The course is designed to equip students for a career in nursing.
Here he received the education that would equip him to take his place in society.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the things that are needed for a particular purpose or activity
examples: a useful piece of equipment for the kitchen
Take care when using old electrical equipment.
electronic/communications/computer equipment
military equipment and supplies
office equipment
They have installed state-of-the-art medical equipment to help improve early diagnosis of the condition.
Everyone should bring the necessary equipment for camping in the mountains.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the process of providing a place or person with necessary things
examples: The equipment of the photographic studio was expensive.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a thing, amount, word, etc. that is equal in value, meaning or purpose to something else
examples: Send €20 or the equivalent in your own currency.
the modern equivalent of the Roman baths
Is there a French word that is the exact equivalent of the English word ‘home’?
Breathing such polluted air is the equivalent of (= has the same effect as) smoking ten cigarettes a day.
The German ‘Gymnasium’ is the closest equivalent to the grammar school in England.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a thing, amount, word, etc. that is equal in value, meaning or purpose to something else
examples: Send €20 or the equivalent in your own currency.
the modern equivalent of the Roman baths
Is there a French word that is the exact equivalent of the English word ‘home’?
Breathing such polluted air is the equivalent of (= has the same effect as) smoking ten cigarettes a day.
The German ‘Gymnasium’ is the closest equivalent to the grammar school in England.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a period of time, usually in history, that is different from other periods because of particular characteristics or events
examples: SEE ALSO Christian era
the Victorian/modern/post-war era
When she left the firm, it was the end of an era (= things were different after that).
This is the start of a new era of peace and prosperity.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a length of time that is a division of an aeonWord Origin
examples: mid 17th cent.: from late Latin aera, denoting a number used as a basis of reckoning, an epoch from which time is reckoned, plural of aes, aer- ‘money, counter’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to build something
examples: The church was erected in 1582.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to put something in position so that it stands upright
examples: SYNONYM put up
Police had to erect barriers to keep crowds back.
to erect a tent

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to create or establish something
examples: to erect trade barriers

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a mistake, especially one that causes problems or affects the result of something
examples: SEE ALSO hard error
spelling/typographical/grammatical errors
The report contains some factual errors that must be corrected.
They committed the fatal error of misjudging the weather conditions.
There are too many errors in your work.
I think you have made an error in calculating the total.
A simple error of judgement meant that there was not enough food to go around.
an error of fact/principle
a serious/grave error
a glaring error (= a mistake that is very obvious)
The computer system was switched off in error (= by mistake.)
There is no room for error in this job.
I get an error message whenever I try to log on.
His attempts to arrange a party ended up as a comedy of errors (= he made so many mistakes it was funny).

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to realize or admit that you have done something wrong and decide to change your behaviour
examples: Will they realize the error of their ways before it is too late?

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: the process of solving a problem by trying various methods until you find a method that is successful
examples: Children learn to use computer programs by trial and error.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: when a volcano erupts or burning rocks, smoke, etc. erupt or are erupted, the burning rocks, etc. are thrown out from the volcano
examples: The volcano could erupt at any time.
Ash began to erupt from the crater.
An immense volume of rocks and molten lava was erupted.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to start happening, suddenly and violently
examples: SYNONYM break out
Violence erupted outside the embassy gates.
The unrest erupted into revolution.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to suddenly express your feelings very strongly, especially by shouting loudly
examples: When Davis scored for the third time the crowd erupted.
My father just erupted into fury.
The room erupted with laughter.
‘How dare you?’ she erupted.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to suddenly appear on your skin
examples: A rash had erupted all over his chest.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to become greater, worse, more serious, etc.; to make something greater, worse, more serious, etc.
examples: the escalating costs of healthcare
The fighting escalated into a full-scale war.
We do not want to escalate the war.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to get away from a place where you have been kept as a prisoner or not allowed to leave
examples: Two prisoners have escaped.
They were caught trying to escape.
He escaped from prison this morning.
She attempted to escaped from the pirates holding her hostage.
She managed to escape her captors.
He escaped prison with two other inmates.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to get away from or avoid something unpleasant or dangerous
examples: Although he had no idea what life there would be like, he had to take the chance to escape.
She managed to escape from the burning car.
As a child he would often escape into a dream world of his own.
We were able to escape to the countryside during the summer months.
I escaped with only minor injuries.
Both drivers escaped unhurt.
to escape unharmed/uninjured/unscathed
She was lucky to escape punishment.
They were glad to have escaped the clutches of winter for another year.
The pilot escaped death by seconds.
There was no escaping the fact that he was overweight.
He narrowly escaped being killed.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to be forgotten or not noticed
examples: Her name escapes me (= I can't remember it).
It might have escaped your notice, but I'm very busy at the moment.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to get out of a container, especially through a hole
examples: Put a lid on to prevent heat escaping.
toxic waste escaping into the sea

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to come out from your mouth without you intending it to
examples: A groan escaped her lips.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to try to prevent or avoid loss or damage when it is already too late to do soWord Origin
examples: Middle English: from Old French eschaper, based on medieval Latin ex- ‘out’ + cappa ‘cloak’. Compare with escapade.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: more with one person, thing, etc. than with others, or more in particular circumstances than in others
examples: SYNONYM particularly
Teenagers are very fashion conscious, especially girls.
I love Rome, especially in the spring.
The car is quite small, especially if you have children.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: for a particular purpose, person, etc.
examples: I got up early especially.
I made it especially for you.
The vehicle was designed especially for use in the desert.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: very much; to a particular degree
examples: A plentiful supply of water is especially important in summer.
especially useful/interesting
Children are expected to obey their parents at all times.This is especially true of girls.
I wasn't feeling especially happy that day.
‘Do you like his novels?’ ‘Not especially.’

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a short piece of writing by a student as part of a course of study
examples: I have to write an essay this weekend.
an essay on the causes of the First World War
Have you done your essay about Napoleon yet?
He made some very good points in his essay.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a short piece of writing on a particular subject, written in order to be published
examples: a collection of essays by prominent African American writers
The book contains a number of interesting essays on women in society.
Pierce contributes a long essay about John F. Kennedy.
I discuss this in a forthcoming essay.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: an attempt to do something
examples: His first essay in politics was a complete disaster.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the most important quality or feature of something, that makes it what it is
examples: His paintings capture the essence of France.
In essence (= when you consider the most important points), your situation isn't so different from mine.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a liquid taken from a plant, etc. that contains its smell and taste in a very strong form
examples: SEE ALSO coffee essence
essence of rose
coffee/vanilla/almond essence

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: necessary and very important
examples: In this situation time is of the essence (= we must do things as quickly as possible).

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: completely necessary; extremely important in a particular situation or for a particular activity
examples: SYNONYM vital
an essential part/feature of something
an essential element/ingredient/component of something
The local government is not able to provide essential services such as gas, water and electricity.
Vitamins play an essential role in many body processes.
The museum is closed while essential repairs are being carried out.
The charity will be taking food and essential supplies to six refugee camps.
This book is essential reading for all nature lovers.
All events are free, but booking is essential.
Money is not essential to happiness.
Experience is essential for this job.
It is essential to keep the two groups separate.
It is absolutely essential for all those involved in education to be computer-literate
It is essential that you have some experience.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: connected with the most important aspect or basic nature of somebody/something
examples: SYNONYM fundamental
The essential difference between Sara and me is in our attitude to money.
He describes what he thinks is the essential nature of America.
The essential character of the town has been destroyed by the new road.
The film captures an essential truth of adolescence

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: when you think about the true, important or basic nature of somebody/something
examples: SYNONYM basically
There are three essentially different ways of tackling the problem.
The pattern is essentially the same in all cases.
Essentially, what we are suggesting is that the firm needs to change.
He was, essentially, a teacher, not a manager.
The article was essentially concerned with her relationship with her parents (= it dealt with other things, but this was the most important).

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to start or create an organization, a system, etc. that is meant to last for a long time
examples: SYNONYM set up
The committee was established in 1912.
They now hope to establish a centre in Cuba.
The company established a base in Florida last year.
to establish a state/government/group/school
to establish standards/principles
Let’s establish some ground rules.
The proposal would establish a system of inspections of prisons worldwide.
They are establishing a network of pumps and pipelines to move the oil.
The new treaty establishes a free trade zone.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to start having a relationship, especially a formal one, with another person, group or country
examples: to establish relations/links/contacts/connections
The school is trying to establish a relationship with the local community.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to hold a position for long enough or succeed in something well enough to make people accept and respect you
examples: He has now firmly established his position in the organization.
The school has established a reputation for academic excellence.
It took him a long time to establish himself.
He has just set up his own business but it will take him a while to get established.
The exhibition helped to establish her as an artist.
By then she was established as a star.
Not long after that she established herself in business.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to make people accept a belief, claim, custom etc.
examples: This success helped to establish the practice of vaccination.
Traditions get established over time.
It was the outbreak of the Second World War that established the tradition of the monarch's Christmas broadcast.
The festival has become established as an annual event.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to discover or prove the facts of a situation
examples: SYNONYM ascertain
Police are still trying to establish the cause of the accident.
There will be an investigation to establish the facts.
We are still trying to establish the identity of the dead man.
His guilt has been clearly established.
The effectiveness of the new drug has not yet been scientifically established.
They have established that his injuries were caused by a fall.
We need to establish where she was at the time of the shooting.
It has since been established that the horse was drugged.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: an organization, a large institution or a hotel
examples: The visa is for foreign nationals wishing to study at a university, college or similar educational establishment.
She's now running a small government research establishment.
The hotel is a comfortable and well-run establishment.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the people in a society or a profession who have influence and power and who usually do not support change
examples: the medical/military/political, etc. establishment
young people rebelling against the Establishment
The members were drawn from the ranks of the Establishment.
orthodox Establishment views

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: the act of starting or creating something that is meant to last for a long time
examples: The speaker announced the establishment of a new college.
His visit facilitated the establishment of diplomatic relations between the countries.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: an area of land with a lot of houses or factories of the same type on it
examples: SEE ALSO council estate
She lives in a tower block on an estate in London.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a large area of land, usually in the country, that is owned by one person or family
examples: a 3 000-acre estate
The poet's childhood was spent on a country estate.
She receives rent from all the people whose cottages are on estate land.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: all the money and property that a person owns, especially everything that is left when they die
examples: Her estate was left to her daughter.
He left estate valued at a million dollars.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: a car with a lot of space behind the back seats and a door at the back for loading large itemsWord Origin
examples: Middle English (in the sense ‘state or condition’): from Old French estat, from Latin status ‘state, condition’, from stare ‘to stand’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to form an idea of the cost, size, value etc. of something, but without calculating it exactly
examples: to estimate the cost/value/number of something
The satellite will cost an estimated £400 million.
Police estimate the crowd at 30 000.
All variables can be estimated from the data.
The number of breeding pairs was estimated as the number of pairs building nests.
The deal is estimated to be worth around $1.5 million.
We estimated (that) it would cost about €5 000.
It is estimated (that) the project will last four years.
It is hard to estimate how many children suffer from dyslexia.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: without an end; existing or continuing forever
examples: the promise of eternal life in heaven
She's an eternal optimist (= she always expects that the best will happen).
eternal truths (= ideas that are always true and never change)
You have my eternal gratitude (= very great gratitude).
To his eternal credit (= very great credit), he never gave up.
Newspapers are simply responding to the eternal fascination of their readers with the private lives of the rich and famous.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: happening often and seeming never to stop
examples: SYNONYM constant
I'm tired of your eternal arguments.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: people never stop hopingWord Origin
examples: late Middle English: via Old French from late Latin aeternalis, from Latin aeternus, from aevum ‘age’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: moral principles that control or influence a person’s behaviour
examples: professional/business/medical ethics
to draw up a code of ethics
He began to question the ethics of his position.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a system of moral principles or rules of behaviour
examples: SEE ALSO Protestant ethic
The ethic of personal achievement is very strong in western societies.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: the branch of philosophy that deals with moral principlesWord Origin
examples: late Middle English (denoting ethics or moral philosophy; also used attributively): from Old French éthique, from Latin ethice, from Greek (hē) ēthikē (tekhnē) ‘(the science of) morals’, based on ēthos ‘nature, disposition’, (plural) ‘customs’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: connected with beliefs and principles about what is right and wrong
examples: ethical issues/standards/questions/dilemmas
the ethical problems of human embryo research

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: morally correct or acceptable
examples: Is it ethical to keep animals in zoos?
It would have been more ethical for him to resign.
ethical investment (= investing money in businesses that are considered morally acceptable)
I don't consider the arms trade to be an ethical one.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: connected with or belonging to a nation or people that shares a cultural tradition
examples: SEE ALSO multi-ethnic
ethnic groups/communities
ethnic strife/tensions/violence (= between people from different races or peoples)
There are continuing ethnic tensions in the region.
ethnic Albanians living in Germany
The country is divided along ethnic lines.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: typical of a country or culture that is very different from modern Western culture and therefore interesting for people in Western countries
examples: ethnic clothes/jewellery/cooking

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the unit of money of some countries of the European Union
examples: I paid five euros for it.
10 million euro
The price is given in euros.
a 30-million-euro deal
A half-kilo pack of pasta costs around 70 euro cents.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: euros as as a system of money; the value of the euro compared with the value of the money of other countries
examples: What if the UK had joined the Euro in 1999?
the value of the euro against the dollar

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to move people from a place of danger to a safer place
examples: Police evacuated nearby buildings.
Children were evacuated from London to escape the bombing.
Families were evacuated to safer parts of the city.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to move out of a place because of danger, and leave the place empty
examples: Employees were urged to evacuate their offices immediately.
Locals were told to evacuate.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to empty your bowelsWord Origin
examples: late Middle English (in the sense ‘clear the contents of’): from Latin evacuat- ‘(of the bowels) emptied’, from the verb evacuare, from e- (variant of ex-) ‘out of’ + vacuus ‘empty’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to form an opinion of the amount, value or quality of something after thinking about it carefully
examples: SYNONYM assess
The trial will evaluate the effectiveness of the different drugs.
Researchers evaluated teaching performance by comparing students' exam results.
The study will critically evaluate whether this technology is useful.
We need to evaluate how well the policy is working.
The cheeses are evaluated for flavour, texture and colour.
Candidates are evaluated on their ability to think independently.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the act of forming an opinion of the amount, value or quality of something after thinking about it carefully
examples: SEE ALSO re-evaluation
an evaluation of the healthcare system
The technique is not widely practised and requires further evaluation.
The discussion includes a critical evaluation of the documentary sources.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used to emphasize something unexpected or surprising
examples: She didn't even call to say she wasn't coming.
He never even opened the letter (= so he certainly didn't read it).
It wouldn't have been possible 30 years ago, maybe even 20.
It was cold there even in summer (= so it must have been very cold in winter).
Even a child can understand it (= so adults certainly can).

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: used when you are comparing things, to make the comparison stronger
examples: You know even less about it than I do.
She's even more intelligent than her sister.
The Second World War made things even worse.
We face an even greater challenge today.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: used to introduce a more exact description of somebody/something
examples: It's an unattractive building, ugly even.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: just at the same time as somebody does something or as something else happens
examples: Even as he shouted the warning the car skidded.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: despite the possibility that; no matter whether
examples: I'll get there, even if I have to walk.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: despite the fact that; even though
examples: He is a great leader, even if he has many enemies.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: despite what has/had happened
examples: I've shown him the photographs but even now he won't believe me.
Even then she would not admit her mistake.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: at this or that exact moment
examples: The troops are even now preparing to march into the city.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: despite that
examples: There are a lot of spelling mistakes; even so, it's quite a good essay.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: despite the fact that
examples: I like her, even though she can be annoying at times.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: despite the fact that; even though
examples: He is a great leader, even if he has many enemies.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: despite what has/had happened
examples: I've shown him the photographs but even now he won't believe me.
Even then she would not admit her mistake.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: at this or that exact moment
examples: The troops are even now preparing to march into the city.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: despite that
examples: There are a lot of spelling mistakes; even so, it's quite a good essay.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: despite the fact that
examples: I like her, even though she can be annoying at times.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the part of the day between the afternoon and the time you go to bed
examples: SEE ALSO good evening
Remember to call me this evening.
We haven't spoken to him since yesterday evening.
I'll see you tomorrow evening.
Come over on Thursday evening.
What do you usually do in the evening?
Mosquitoes usually bite in the early evening.
She's going to her sister's for the evening.
on the evening of May 15
He hardly spoke throughout the evening.
We spent many enjoyable summer evenings together.
I found it in the pocket of the jacket I had been wearing the previous evening.
The evening meal is served at 7 p.m.
She watched the evening news at 6 p.m. as usual.
As the evening wore on, Sam became more and more unhappy.
Jim's comedy routine was the highlight of the evening's entertainment.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: an event of a particular type happening in the evening
examples: a musical evening at school (= when music is performed)
the school parents' evening (= when parents are invited to talk to teachers about their children's progress)

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a thing that happens, especially something important
examples: recent/current/world events
The tragic events of last Monday occurred only 200 metres from the shore.
Historians long ago established that the event never happened.
TV viewers watched in horror as events unfolded.
a dramatic turn of events (= change in what is happening)
Everyone was frightened by the strange sequence of events.
The police have reconstructed the chain of events leading to the murder.
an unfortunate series of events
Why should we believe his version of events (= description of what happened from his point of view)?
The decisions we take now may influence the course of events (= the way things happen) in the future.
In the normal course of events (= if things had happened as expected) she would have gone with him.
He found that the report he had written had been overtaken by events (= it was no longer relevant).
A minority of patients suffered adverse events, including heart attacks.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a planned public or social occasion
examples: SEE ALSO non-event
Is the city ready to host such a major sporting event?
The hospital is organizing a special fundraising event.
They were invited to attend the social event of the year.
As always, the annual event will be held in the grounds of the house.
Events are taking place throughout the summer to celebrate the city's centenary.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: one of the races or competitions in a sports programme
examples: SEE ALSO field event
The 800 metres is the fourth event of the afternoon.
Local winners compete in a national event in September.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: after something has happened
examples: I knew nothing about it until after the event.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to understand something, or realize what you should have done, only after something has happened
examples: Anyone can be wise after the event.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: the birth of a baby

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: used to emphasize or show that something is true or will happen despite other circumstances
examples: SYNONYM in any case
I think she'll agree to do it but in any event, all she can say is ‘no’.
I think the economy will recover in any event.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: when the situation actually happened
examples: I got very nervous about the exam, but in the event, I needn't have worried; it was really easy.
In the event though, the dinner was a very entertaining affair.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: if something happens
examples: In the event of an accident, call this number.
Sheila will inherit everything in the event of his death.
In the unlikely event of a crash, please remain calm.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: if that happens
examples: In that event, we will have to reconsider our offer.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: at the end of a period of time or a series of events
examples: Our flight eventually left five hours late.
I'll get round to mending it eventually.
She hopes eventually to attend medical school and become a doctor.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used in negative sentences and questions, or sentences with if to mean ‘at any time’
examples: Nothing ever happens here.
Don't you ever get tired?
If you're ever in Miami, come and see us.
‘Have you ever been to Rome?’ ‘Yes, I have, actually. Not long ago.’
‘Have you ever thought of changing your job?’ ‘No, never/No I haven’t.’
She hardly ever (= almost never) goes out.
We've only ever talked on the phone.
I don't think I ever really thanked you properly.
He wondered whether it would ever actually happen.
We see them very seldom, if ever.
I'll never ever do that again!
I'm never speaking to you ever again!

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: used for emphasis when you are comparing things
examples: SEE ALSO first-ever
It was raining harder than ever.
Consumers today have more choices than ever before.
It's my best ever score.
It's the worst film I've ever seen.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: all the time or every time; always
examples: SEE ALSO forever
Paul, ever the optimist, agreed to try again.
She married the prince and they lived happily ever after.
He said he would love her for ever (and ever).
Their debts grew ever larger (= kept increasing).
the ever-growing problem
an ever-present danger

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: used after when, why, etc. to show that you are surprised or shocked
examples: Why ever did you agree?

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: used to emphasize that somebody does the same thing very often, usually in an annoying way
examples: All he ever does is grumble about things.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: used to show that you are surprised or shocked
examples: Did you ever hear anything like it?

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: continuously since the time mentioned
examples: He's had a car ever since he was 18.
I was bitten by a dog once and I've been afraid of them ever since.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: very; really
examples: He looks ever so smart.
She's ever such a nice woman.
It's ever so easy.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: used to emphasize that something is certainly true
examples: That was a disaster if ever there was one!

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: used to emphasize something you are talking about
examples: ‘You must have been upset by that.’ ‘Was I ever!’

definitions.label: Meaning 11
definitions.definition: sometimes used at the end of an informal letter, before you write your nameWord Origin
examples: Old English ǣfre, of unknown origin.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used with singular nouns to refer to all the members of a group of things or people
examples: She knows every student in the school.
I could hear every word they said.
We enjoyed every minute of our stay.
I go to the gym every day.
every week/month/year
I get that wrong every single time.
I read every last article in the newspaper (= all of them).
They were watching her every movement.
Every one of their songs has been a hit.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: used to say how often something happens or is done
examples: The buses go every 10 minutes.
We had to stop every few miles.
One in every three marriages ends in divorce.
He has every third day off (= he works for two days, then has one day off, then works for two days and so on).
We see each other every now and again.
Every now and then he regretted his decision.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: all possible
examples: We wish you every success.
He had every reason to be angry.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: every single one
examples: I look forward to seeing each and every one of you as we celebrate our 50th year.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: each alternate one (= the first, third, fifth, etc. one, but not the second, fourth, sixth, etc.)
examples: They visit us every other week.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: every person; all people
examples: COMPARE anybody
Everybody knows Tom.
Have you asked everybody?
Didn't you like it? Everybody else did.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used or happening every day or regularly; ordinary
examples: Change is a part of everyday life in business.
plates and dishes for everyday use
Using everyday objects, basic scientific principles can be explained to young children.
Violent crime is part of the everyday experience of the people in these neighbourhoods.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: every person; all people
examples: Everyone cheered and clapped.
Everyone has a chance to win.
Everyone brought their partner to the party.
Everyone brought his or her partner to the party.
The police questioned everyone in the room.
The teacher commented on everyone's work.
Everyone else was there.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: all things
examples: Everything had gone.
When we confronted him, he denied everything.
Take this bag, and leave everything else to me.
She seemed to have everything—looks, money, intelligence.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the situation now; life generally
examples: Everything in the capital is now quiet.
‘How's everything with you?’ ‘Fine, thanks.’

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: the most important thing
examples: Money isn't everything.
My family means everything to me.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: and so on; and other similar things
examples: Have you got his name and address and everything?
She told me about the baby and everything.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: in, to or at every place; all places
examples: I've looked everywhere.
He follows me everywhere.
We'll have to eat here—everywhere else is full.
Everywhere we went was full of tourists.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the facts, signs or objects that make you believe that something is true
examples: Researchers have found clear scientific evidence of a link between exposure to sun and skin cancer.
There is a growing body of evidence for the existence of black holes that are ten times as massive as the Sun.
There is not a shred of evidence that the meeting actually took place.
Have you any evidence to support this allegation?
The study provides empirical evidence (= based on experiments or experience) to prove that the drug has no long-term side effects.
Anecdotal evidence (= based on personal accounts) suggests that drivers over the age of 70 find it difficult to get insurance.
On the evidence of their recent matches, it is unlikely the Spanish team will win.
In the absence of evidence to the contrary, it should be assumed that proper procedures were followed.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the information that is used in court to try to prove something
examples: SEE ALSO circumstantial
I was asked to give evidence (= to say what I knew, describe what I had seen, etc.) at the trial.
The defence accused the prosecution of withholding several key pieces of evidence.
circumstantial/forensic evidence
Despite a lack of evidence against him, Burton will appear in court next week.
He was released when the judge ruled there was no evidence against him.
The emails were presented as evidence of his involvement in the fraud.
The police officer took a statement which was later used in evidence.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: (considering) the evidence on both sides of an argument, to find the most likely reason for or result of something
examples: The balance of evidence suggests the Liberal party's decline began before the First World War.
The coroner thought that on the balance of probabilities, the pilot had suffered a stroke just before the crash.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: (to be) present and clearly seen
examples: The police were much in evidence at today's demonstration.
a trend that has been much in evidence in recent years

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: clear; easily seen
examples: SYNONYM obvious
The orchestra played with evident enjoyment.
It has now become evident to us that a mistake has been made.
The growing interest in history is clearly evident in the number of people visiting museums and country houses.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: enjoying harming others; morally bad and cruel
examples: Police described the killer as ‘a desperate and evil man’.
an evil genius/dictator
President Reagan referred to the Soviet Union as the ‘evil empire’.
an evil grin
Her face was full of evil intent.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: having a harmful effect on people; morally bad
examples: evil deeds
In his speech he described the evil effects of racism.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: connected with the devil and with what is bad in the world
examples: It was an ancient charm to ward off evil spirits.
She had been deceived by an evil demon.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: extremely unpleasant
examples: The rubbish bin was giving off an evil smell.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: the time when you have to do something difficult or unpleasant
examples: I’d better go and see the dentist—I can’t put off the evil hour any longer.
If you keep on borrowing, you are only postponing the evil day when you have to pay it all back.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: a person or spirit who is thought to have a good/bad influence over you

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: an unpleasant drink that is a mixture of different thingsWord Origin
examples: Old English yfel, of Germanic origin; related to Dutch euvel and German Übel.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: enjoying harming others; morally bad and cruel
examples: Police described the killer as ‘a desperate and evil man’.
an evil genius/dictator
President Reagan referred to the Soviet Union as the ‘evil empire’.
an evil grin
Her face was full of evil intent.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: having a harmful effect on people; morally bad

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: connected with the devil and with what is bad in the world
examples: It was an ancient charm to ward off evil spirits.
She had been deceived by an evil demon.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: extremely unpleasant
examples: The rubbish bin was giving off an evil smell.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: the time when you have to do something difficult or unpleasant
examples: I’d better go and see the dentist—I can’t put off the evil hour any longer.
If you keep on borrowing, you are only postponing the evil day when you have to pay it all back.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: a person or spirit who is thought to have a good/bad influence over you

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: an unpleasant drink that is a mixture of different thingsWord Origin
examples: Old English yfel, of Germanic origin; related to Dutch euvel and German Übel.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to bring a feeling, a memory or an image into your mind
examples: The music evoked memories of her youth.
His case is unlikely to evoke public sympathy.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the slow steady development of plants, animals, etc. during the history of the earth, as they adapt to changes in their environment
examples: the evolution of the human species
Darwin’s theory of evolution
Finally it was legal to teach evolution everywhere in America.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the slow steady development of something
examples: In politics Britain has preferred evolution to revolution (= slow steady development to sudden violent change)
cultural trends and evolutions

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: connected with evolution; connected with slow steady development and change
examples: evolutionary theory
evolutionary change

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to develop gradually, especially from a simple to a more complicated form; to develop something in this way
examples: The idea evolved from a drawing I discovered in the attic.
The company has evolved into a major chemical manufacturer.
Each school must evolve its own way of working.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to develop over time, often many generations, into forms that are better adapted to survive changes in their environment
examples: The three species evolved from a single ancestor.
The dolphin has evolved a highly developed jaw.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: correct in every detail
examples: SYNONYM precise
The new palace is an exact replica of the original building.
It is an exact copy of the original document.
The model is exact in every detail.
For now they are keeping the exact date and location of the wedding a secret.
The exact nature of her illness (= precisely what her illness is) has not been made public.
Her second husband was the exact opposite of her first (= completely different).
The colours were an almost exact match.
She's in her mid-thirties—thirty-six to be exact.
I had the exact same problem as you when I first started.
What were his exact words?
A clear definition requires very exact wording.
Nobody knows the exact number of people affected, but it is over 10 000.
He started to phone me at the exact moment I started to phone him (= at the same time).

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: very accurate and careful about details
examples: SYNONYM meticulous
He was very exact about everything he did.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: using accurate measurements and following set rules
examples: SYNONYM precise
Assessing insurance risk can never be an exact science.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used to emphasize that something is correct in every way or in every detail
examples: SYNONYM precisely
It's exactly nine o'clock.
It happened almost exactly a year ago.
Your answer is exactly right.
It was a warm day, if not exactly hot.
I know exactly how she felt.
It's impossible to say exactly what happened.
Do exactly as I tell you.
You haven't changed at all—you still look exactly the same.
His words had exactly the opposite effect.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: used to ask for more information about something
examples: Where exactly did you stay in France?
Exactly what are you trying to tell me?

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: used as a reply, agreeing with what somebody has just said, or emphasizing that it is correct
examples: ‘You mean somebody in this room must be the murderer?’ ‘Exactly.’

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: used when you are saying the opposite of what you really mean
examples: He wasn't exactly pleased to see us—in fact he refused to open the door.
It's not exactly beautiful, is it? (= it's ugly)

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: used when you are correcting something that somebody has said
examples: ‘So he told you you'd got the job?’ ‘Not exactly, but he said they were impressed with me.’

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to make something seem larger, better, worse or more important than it really is
examples: The hotel was really filthy and I'm not exaggerating.
He tends to exaggerate the difficulties.
I'm sure he exaggerates his Irish accent (= tries to sound more Irish than he really is).
Demand for the product has been greatly exaggerated.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a formal written, spoken or practical test, especially at school or college, to see how much you know about a subject, or what you can do
examples: SEE ALSO exit exam
to take an exam
to pass/fail an exam
I hate doing exams.
to sit an exam
to mark an exam
to grade an exam
I failed the college entrance exam (= to get a place at college).
Every term we would have exams in maths, English, French, etc.
She did well in her exams.
She did well on her exams.
an exam paper
I got my exam results today.
A lot of students suffer from exam nerves.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a medical test of a particular part of the body
examples: an eye exam

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a formal written, spoken or practical test, especially at school or college, to see how much you know about a subject, or what you can do
examples: successful candidates in GCSE examinations
to sit an examination in mathematics
In 1864 he passed the examination for the Indian Civil Service.
Applicants are selected for jobs on the results of a competitive examination.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the act of looking at or considering something very carefully
examples: Careful examination of the ruins revealed an even earlier temple.
The issue needs further examination.
The review is the most detailed examination of policing since 1992.
The chapter concludes with a brief examination of some of the factors causing family break-up.
After a thorough examination, they announced that the suspicious device was harmless.
On closer examination it was found that the signature was not genuine.
Your proposals are still under examination.
The party would open up the issue to examination by a Senate Committee.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a close look at something/somebody, especially to see if there is anything wrong or to find the cause of a problem
examples: SEE ALSO cross-examination
a medical/physical examination
a post-mortem/forensic examination
Regular breast examination is advised.
A specialist should carry out an examination of the patient.
Diagnosis can be made only by direct examination of affected brain tissue.
Further examination by an orthopaedic surgeon will be needed today.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to consider or study an idea, a subject, etc. very carefully
examples: SEE ALSO re-examine
This study sets out to examine in detail the possible effects of climate change.
Her new show critically examines the relationship between the arts and popular culture.
This important issue must be carefully examined.
Only recently have historians begun to examine the impact and influence of these changes.
It is necessary to examine how the proposals can be carried out.
The weather gave researchers an opportunity to examine what happens to insect numbers when temperatures rise.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to look at somebody/something closely, to see if there is anything wrong or to find the cause of a problem
examples: The doctor examined her carefully but could find nothing wrong.
to be examined by a doctor/psychiatrist/specialist/vet
She examined herself closely in the mirror.
The samples were examined under the microscope for the presence of damaged cells.
The goods were examined for damage on arrival.
Investigators examined the room minutely for clues.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to give somebody a test to see how much they know about a subject or what they can do
examples: The students will be examined in all subjects at the end of term.
You are only being examined on this semester's work.
The course is externally examined (= arranged and marked by somebody from outside a school, a university or an organization).

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to ask somebody questions formally, especially in court
examples: SEE ALSO cross-examine
The prosecution examined 20 witnesses.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to be crazyWord Origin
examples: Middle English: from Old French examiner, from Latin examinare ‘weigh, test’, from examen ‘examination’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: something such as an object, a fact or a situation that shows, explains or supports what you say
examples: Let me give you an example.
It is important to cite examples to support your argument.
to provide/offer an example
I shall take four different examples from contemporary literature to illustrate my point.
Can you show me an example of what you mean?
This dictionary has many examples of how words are used.
Just to give you an example of his generosity—he gave me his old car and wouldn't take any money for it.
The progress the students have made serves as an example of the benefit of small class sizes.
By way of example, we'll look at our most recent advertising campaign.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a thing that is typical of or represents a particular group or set
examples: This is a good example of the artist's early work.
It is a perfect example of this type of architecture.
Japan is often quoted as the prime example of a modern industrial nation.
It is a classic example of how not to design a new city centre.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a person or their behaviour that is thought to be a good model for others to copy
examples: Her courage is an example to us all.
He sets an example for the other students.
She is a shining example of what people with disabilities can achieve.
He is a captain who leads by example.
Top management should be seen to lead by example.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: a person’s behaviour, either good or bad, that other people copy
examples: It would be a mistake to follow his example.
They started to plan protests, inspired by the example of their neighbours.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: used to emphasize something that explains or supports what you are saying; used to give an example of what you are saying
examples: There is a similar word in many languages, for example in French and Italian.
The report is incomplete; it does not include sales in France, for example.
It is possible to combine computer science with other subjects, for example physics.
An athlete, for example, might turn the pedals 80 times a minute.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to punish somebody as a warning to others not to do the same thing
examples: The teacher made an example of him by suspending him from school.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to be greater than a particular number or amount
examples: The price will not exceed £100.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to do more than the law or an order, etc. allows you to do
examples: SEE ALSO excess
She was exceeding the speed limit (= driving faster than is allowed).
The officers had exceeded their authority.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to be better than expected
examples: SYNONYM surpass
His achievements have exceeded expectations.
The amount raised has far exceeded our wildest expectations.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the quality of being extremely good
examples: SEE ALSO par excellence
a reputation for academic excellence
The hospital is recognized as a centre of excellence in research and teaching.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: extremely good
examples: SEE ALSO xlnt
an excellent book/article
excellent results/work
The meal looked and tasted excellent.
Both the food and the service were truly excellent.
The performances of the cast are uniformly excellent throughout.
She has done an excellent job of adapting the novel for the screen.
It is an excellent example of how a farm can work in harmony with nature.
The party provided an excellent opportunity to meet new people.
The apartment is in excellent condition and is ready to move into.
He was great at sport and excellent at art.
Our staff are excellent at advising small businesses.
The experience was excellent for students' self-confidence.
Ferns are excellent for planting in shady parts of the garden.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: used to show that you are very pleased about something or that you approve of something
examples: You can all come? Excellent!
It's excellent to see so many people at today's event!

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used before you mention the only thing or person about which a statement is not true
examples: SYNONYM apart from
We work every day except Sunday.
They all came except Matt.
I had nothing on except for my socks.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used before you mention the only thing or person about which a statement is not true
examples: SYNONYM apart from
We work every day except Sunday.
They all came except Matt.
I had nothing on except for my socks.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a person or thing that is not included in a general statement
examples: Most of the buildings in the town are modern, but the church is an exception.
With very few exceptions, private schools get the best exam results.
Nobody had much money at the time and I was no exception.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a thing that does not follow a rule
examples: Good writing is unfortunately the exception rather than the rule (= it is unusual).
There are always a lot of exceptions to grammar rules.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: people say that something is the exception that proves the rule when they are stating something that seems to be different from the normal situation, but they mean that the normal situation remains true in general
examples: Most electronics companies have not done well this year, but ours is the exception that proves the rule.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to allow somebody not to follow the usual rule on one occasion or for one particular reason
examples: Children are not usually allowed in, but I'm prepared to make an exception in this case.
No parking is allowed, but an exception is made for disabled drivers.
We are making a special exception for Emma because of her condition.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to object strongly to something; to be angry about something
examples: I take great exception to the fact that you told my wife before you told me.
No one could possibly take exception to his comments.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: except; not including
examples: All his novels are set in Italy with the exception of his last.
The whole of the island was flooded with the exception of a small area in the north.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: used to emphasize that the statement you are making is always true and everyone or everything is included
examples: All students without exception must take the English examination.
Without exception, all employees must carry their identity card with them at all times.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: unusually good
examples: SYNONYM outstanding
At the age of five he showed exceptional talent as a musician.
The quality of the recording is quite exceptional.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: very unusual
examples: OPPOSITE unexceptional
This deadline will be extended only in exceptional circumstances.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: more than is necessary, reasonable or acceptable
examples: You can throw away any excess.
Are you suffering from an excess of stress in your life?
In an excess of enthusiasm I agreed to work late.
He started drinking to excess after losing his job.
The increase will not be in excess of (= more than) two per cent.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: an amount by which something is larger than something else
examples: We cover costs up to £600 and then you pay the excess.

definitions.label: Meaning 3

That's not the sort of behaviour I expect of you!

definitions.label: Meaning 2

They are not expected until tomorrow.
Are you expecting visitors?

We were expecting him to arrive yesterday.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to demand that somebody will do something because it is their duty or responsibility
examples: It is reasonable to expect changes in the way we work.

He's still getting over his illness, so it's unrealistic to expect too much from him.
Are you clear what is expected of you?

We are expected to work on Saturdays.
It would be unreasonable to expect them to do all that work for free.
I expect to be paid promptly for the work.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: used when you think something is probably true
examples: ‘Will you be late?’ ‘I expect so.’
‘Are you going out tonight?’ ‘I don't expect so.’
‘Who’s eaten all the cake?’ ‘Tom, I expect/I expect it was Tom.’

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to be pregnant
examples: Ann's expecting a baby in June.
I didn't know she was expecting!

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to be likely to happen; to be quite normal
examples: A little tiredness after taking these drugs is to be expected.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: used to tell somebody not to be surprised by something
examples: She swore at you? What do you expect when you treat her like that?

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a belief that something will happen because it is likely

I applied for the post more in hope than expectation.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a hope that something good will happen
examples: She went to college with great expectations.

I don't want to raise your expectations too much.

The numbers attending fell short of expectations.

definitions.label: Meaning 3

examples: Unfortunately the new software has failed to meet expectations.

definitions.label: Meaning 1

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the people who go on an expedition
examples: Three members of the Everest expedition were killed.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a short trip that you make when you want or need something
examples: Win a fantastic shopping expedition to New York!

definitions.label: Meaning 1

examples: a reduction in public/government/military expenditure
plans to increase expenditure on health

Savings have been disposed of in order to meet the growing gap between income and expenditure.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the use of energy, time, materials, etc.
examples: the expenditure of emotion
This study represents a major expenditure of time and effort.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the money that you spend on something
examples: The garden was transformed at great expense.
No expense was spared (= they spent as much money as was needed) to make the party a success.
He's arranged everything, no expense spared.
She always travels first-class regardless of expense.
The results are well worth the expense.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: something that makes you spend money
examples: Running a car is a big expense.
The company views its workers as an expense instead of an asset.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: money spent in doing a particular job, or for a particular purpose
examples: living/medical/travel expenses
legal/household expenses
The company has cut operating expenses to their lowest levels in three years
Can I give you something towards expenses?
financial help to meet the expenses of an emergency
The payments he gets barely cover his expenses.
Property investors are entitled to offset the expenses incurred buying the property.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: money that you spend while you are working and that your employer will pay back to you later
examples: You can claim back your travelling/travel expenses.
We paid their expenses, but nothing more.
an all-expenses-paid trip
to take a client out for a meal on expenses

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: paid for by somebody
examples: We were taken out for a meal at the company's expense.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: if you make a joke at somebody’s expense, you laugh at them and make them feel silly

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: with loss or damage to somebody/something
examples: He built up the business at the expense of his health.
an education system that benefits bright children at the expense of those who are slower to learn

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to spend money on something
examples: They went to all the expense of redecorating the house and then they moved.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to make somebody spend money on something
examples: Their visit put us to a lot of expense.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: costing a lot of money
examples: OPPOSITE cheap (1)
an expensive car/restaurant/holiday
I can't afford it—it's too expensive.
Making the wrong decision could prove expensive.
That dress was an expensive mistake.
Art books are expensive to produce.
The new regulations are likely to be very expensive for employers.
Bonds can be expensive for individuals to invest in.
It's expensive to live in London.
It is now more expensive for Europeans to visit here.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the knowledge and skill that you have gained through doing something for a period of time; the process of gaining this
examples: SEE ALSO work experience
My lack of practical experience was a disadvantage.
Do you have any previous experience of this type of work?
This new approach draws on years of experience of teaching children to read.
a doctor with experience in dealing with patients suffering from stress
He gained extensive experience in the field of artificial intelligence whilst working on the project.
I have over ten years’ experience as a teacher.
The course provides hands-on experience with various systems.
She didn't get paid much but it was all good experience.
We all learn by experience.
The new player will bring a wealth of experience to the team.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the things that have happened to you that influence the way you think and behave
examples: Experience has taught me that life can be very unfair.
Experience shows that this strategy does not always work.
The book is based on personal experience.
It is important to try and learn from experience.
She knew from past experience that Ann would not give up easily.
In my experience, very few people really understand the problem.
He had first-hand experience of poverty.
the collective experience of everyday life

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: an event or activity that affects you in some way
examples: SEE ALSO near-death experience
a unique/positive/wonderful experience
Share your experiences of parenthood by emailing the address below.
We aim to give our guests the experience of a lifetime.
It was her first experience of living alone.
The play is based loosely on his own life experiences.
He found the whole experience traumatic.
Losing four matches in a row proved a valuable learning experience (= it showed the players what they need to improve).
Living in Africa was very different from home and quite an experience (= unusual for us).

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: what it is like for somebody to use a service, do an activity, attend an event, etc.
examples: SEE ALSO user experience
We are continually looking for ways to improve the customer experience.
Enjoy a fine dining experience with quality service.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: events or knowledge shared by all the members of a particular group in society, that influences the way they think and behave
examples: musical forms like jazz that emerged out of the Black American experience

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: used to say that somebody should think of a failure as being something that they can learn from
examples: We lost a lot of money, but we just put it down to experience.

definitions.label: Meaning 4

definitions.label: Meaning 8

definitions.label: Meaning 1

definitions.label: Meaning 2

She expresses herself most fully in her paintings.

definitions.label: Meaning 3

definitions.label: Meaning 4

definitions.label: Meaning 6

The poet's anger finds expression in (= is shown in) the last verse of the poem.

expressions of concern/sympathy/support

laws which aim to restrict free expression of opinion

definitions.label: Meaning 3

He looked down at the tiny child and his expression softened.
His expression changed from surprise to one of amusement.
Her expression betrayed nothing of her thoughts.

definitions.label: Meaning 4

examples: Try to put a little more expression into it!

definitions.label: Meaning 5

examples: late Middle English: from Latin expressio(n-), from exprimere ‘press out, express’. Compare with express(verb).

definitions.label: Meaning 1

definitions.label: Meaning 3

examples: We have an extension in the bedroom.

definitions.label: Meaning 6

definitions.label: Meaning 7

definitions.label: Meaning 8

definitions.label: Meaning 63
