definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: an official order that limits trade, contact, etc. with a particular country, in order to make it do something, such as obeying international law
examples: Trade sanctions were imposed against any country that refused to sign the agreement.
The economic sanctions have been lifted.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: official permission or approval for an action or a change
examples: SYNONYM authorization
These changes will require the sanction of the court.
Their ideas received official sanction at the meeting.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a course of action that can be used, if necessary, to make people obey a law or behave in a particular way
examples: SYNONYM penalty
The ultimate sanction will be the closure of the restaurant.
We now have an effective sanction against the killing of whales.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a substance that consists of very small fine grains of rock. Sand is found on beaches, in deserts, etc.
examples: a grain of sand
coarse/fine sand
Concrete is a mixture of sand and cement.
The children were playing in the sand (= for example, in a sandpit).
The resort has its own white sand beach.
His hair was the colour of sand.
The beach is a gorgeous stretch of golden sand.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a large area of sand on a beach or in the desert
examples: We went for a walk along the sand.
miles of golden sands
the burning desert sands

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to refuse to admit that a problem exists or refuse to deal with it

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: (to establish) a clear limit to what you will do or accept
examples: It’s time to draw a line in the sand and stop allowing workplace bullying to continue.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: used to describe a situation that changes so often that it is difficult to understand or deal with itWord Origin
examples: Old English, of Germanic origin; related to Dutch zand and German Sand.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: two slices of bread, often spread with butter, with a layer of meat, cheese, etc. between them
examples: SEE ALSO club sandwich
a ham/tuna/egg sandwich
a grilled cheese sandwich
a toasted sandwich
a sandwich bar (= a place that sells sandwiches)
I'm going to grab a sandwich (= buy one quickly) and sit in the park.
We ate turkey sandwiches and wild blueberries.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a sponge cake consisting of two layers with jam and/or cream between them
examples: a chocolate sponge sandwich
a sandwich tin (= for baking such a cake in)

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: an electronic device that is sent into space and moves around the earth or another planet. It is used for communicating by radio, television, etc. and for gathering information.
examples: a weather/communications/spy satellite
The interview came live by satellite from Hollywood.
They could track the tagged sea turtles by satellite.
The information was sent via a satellite link.
satellite television/TV/radio (= broadcast using a satellite)
a satellite broadcast/channel/picture
The use of satellite phones meant that journalists could report directly from the arena of the battlefront.
My car was fitted with a satellite navigation system.
The software enables the user to set up a satellite communications link.
They have successfully launched satellites into orbit.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a natural object that moves around a larger natural object in space
examples: The moon is a satellite of earth.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a town, a country or an organization that is controlled by and depends on another larger or more powerful one
examples: Following the Second World War it became a satellite state of the Soviet Union.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the good feeling that you have when you have achieved something or when something that you wanted to happen does happen; something that gives you this feeling
examples: SEE ALSO dissatisfaction
to gain/get/derive satisfaction from something
a look/smile of satisfaction
She looked back on her career with great satisfaction.
He had the satisfaction of seeing his book become a bestseller.
She didn't want to give him the satisfaction of seeing her cry.
The company is trying to improve customer satisfaction.
He was enjoying all the satisfactions of being a parent.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the act of fulfilling a need or desire
examples: the satisfaction of sexual desires
the satisfaction of your ambitions

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: an acceptable way of dealing with a complaint, a debt, an injury, etc.
examples: I complained to the manager but I didn't get any satisfaction.
They agreed on a payment of £200 in full satisfaction of the debt.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: if you do something to somebody’s satisfaction, they are pleased with it
examples: The affair was settled to the complete satisfaction of the client.
The matter was resolved to our general satisfaction.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: if you prove something to somebody’s satisfaction, they believe or accept it
examples: Can you demonstrate to our satisfaction that your story is true?

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: pleased because you have achieved something or because something that you wanted to happen has happened
examples: OPPOSITE dissatisfied
a satisfied customer
a satisfied smile
She's never satisfied with what she's got.
The Olympic athlete was satisfied with her performance.
They were not satisfied with the outcome of the talks.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: believing or accepting that something is true
examples: SYNONYM convinced
I'm satisfied that they are telling the truth.
Police were satisfied that the death was accidental.
I am quite satisfied he will return to France.
She seemed satisfied with my explanation.
The police are not satisfied with the answers they have received.
We are still not entirely satisfied with the explanation offered.
You need to be satisfied of all the facts.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to make somebody pleased by doing or giving them what they want
examples: Nothing satisfies him—he's always complaining.
The proposed plan will not satisfy everyone.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to provide what is wanted, needed or asked for
examples: The food wasn't enough to satisfy his hunger.
to satisfy somebody’s curiosity
The education system must satisfy the needs of all children.
We cannot satisfy demand for the product.
to satisfy a requirement/condition/criterion
She failed to satisfy all the requirements for entry to the college.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to make somebody certain something is true or has been done
examples: Her explanation did not satisfy the teacher.
People need to be satisfied of the need for a new system.
Once I had satisfied myself (that) it was the right decision, we went ahead.
All you have to do is satisfy the court he is not at risk.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the day of the week after Friday and before Sunday
examples: It's Saturday today, isn't it?
She started art classes last Saturday.
Are you busy next Saturday?
Saturday morning/afternoon/evening
We'll chat at Saturday's party.
I work Saturday to Wednesday.
I work Saturdays to Wednesdays.
We'll meet on Saturday (= next Saturday).
We met on Saturday (= last Saturday).
We'll meet Saturday.
The office is closed on Saturdays (= every Saturday).
The office is closed Saturdays.
He was born on a Saturday.
I always do yoga on a Saturday (= every Saturday).
I went to Mexico City on Monday, and came back the following Saturday.
‘When did the accident happen?’ ‘It was the Saturday (= the Saturday of the week we are talking about).’
Come back Saturday week (= a week after next Saturday).

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a thick liquid that is eaten with food to add taste to it
examples: SEE ALSO apple sauce
tomato/cranberry/chilli sauce
chicken in a white sauce
ice cream with a hot fudge sauce
pasta sauce (= sauce that is served with pasta)
A honey-mustard dipping sauce helped add flavour to the crab cakes.
coconut tart served with hot chocolate sauce

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: talk or behaviour that is annoying or shows no respect
examples: SYNONYM cheek

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: what one person is allowed to do, another person must be allowed to do in a similar situationWord Origin
examples: Middle English: from Old French, based on Latin salsus ‘salted’, past participle of salere ‘to salt’, from sal ‘salt’. Compare with salad.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to keep somebody/something safe from death, harm, loss, etc.
examples: to save somebody’s life
Doctors were unable to save her.
He's trying to save their marriage.
She needs to win the next two games to save the match.
Workers chose longer hours in order to save jobs.
If you really want to save the planet, sell your car.
Thanks for doing that. You saved my life (= helped me a lot).
She started a campaign to save her business.
to save a rare species from extinction
His intrepid act saved five men from death.
Money from local businesses helped save the school from closure.
This new technology might just have the power to save the world from ecological disaster.
She saved a little girl from falling into the water.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to keep money instead of spending it, especially in order to buy a particular thing
examples: I'm not very good at saving.
We scrimp and save to send our children to a private school.
I'm saving up to buy a new car.
I'm saving for a new bike.
For all younger people in the US saving for retirement will be an absolute necessity.
We've been saving up to go to Australia.
I'm trying to save up for my holiday.
You should save a little each week.
I've saved almost £100 so far.
He saved up some money and made plans to travel.
He's been saving his allowance up for a new bike.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to avoid wasting something or using more than necessary
examples: People are looking for ways to save money.
We'll take a cab to save time.
Recycling waste saves energy.
Images are captured in black and white to save hard disk space.
Book early and save £50!
We should try to save water.
The government is trying to save £1 million on defence.
If we go this way it will save us two hours on the trip.
A professional wedding coordinator can save you time and money.
I save on fares by walking to work.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to keep something to use or enjoy in the future or for somebody else to use
examples: He's saving his strength for the last part of the race.
We'll eat some now and save some for tomorrow.
Save some food for me.
The main event is saved until last.
Save me some food.
I won't save you a seat if you're late.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to make a computer keep data by putting a copy in a location where it will be stored
examples: We recommend you save regularly by clicking on the update button.
Save data frequently.
All your recent searches are automatically saved.
The data can be saved to disk.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to collect something because you like it or for a special purpose
examples: I've been saving theatre programmes for years.
If you save ten tokens you can get a T-shirt.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to avoid doing something difficult or unpleasant; to make somebody able to avoid doing something difficult or unpleasant
examples: The prize money saved her from having to find a job.
She did it herself to save argument.

definitions.label: Meaning 10

definitions.label: Meaning 11

definitions.label: Meaning 13

definitions.label: Meaning 14

You can scratch my name off the list.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to make an annoying noise by rubbing something with something sharp
examples: His pen scratched away on the paper.
We could hear mice scratching behind the wall.
The dog kept scratching at the door to go out.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to make enough money to live on, but with difficulty
examples: 75% of the population scratch a living from the soil.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to decide that something cannot happen or somebody/something cannot take part in something, before it starts
examples: to scratch a rocket launch
The horse was scratched from the race because of injury.
She had scratched because of a knee injury.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to think hard in order to find an answer to something
examples: Experts have been scratching their heads over the increase in teenage crime.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to deal with, understand, or find out about only a small part of a subject or problem

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: used to say that if somebody helps you, you will help them, even if this is unfair to othersWord Origin

definitions.label: Meaning 1

The kids were screaming with excitement.
I screamed in pain.
The man screamed in agony and collapsed.

People ran for the exits, screaming out in terror.

The baby was screaming itself hoarse.
screaming fans

He screamed at me to stop.

She screamed abuse at him.
She screamed out abuse at him.

He screamed his head off (= screamed very loudly and angrily) at me.
His sister screamed out that he was crazy.

definitions.label: Meaning 3

examples: SYNONYM screech
Lights flashed and sirens screamed.
The powerboat screamed out to sea.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: if you drag somebody kicking and screaming to do something, they only do it with great protests because they don't really want to do it at all
examples: The president had to be dragged kicking and screaming to the signing ceremony.

definitions.label: Meaning 5

examples: Middle English: origin uncertain; perhaps from Middle Dutch.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the flat surface at the front of a television, computer, or other electronic device, on which you see pictures or information
examples: SEE ALSO flat-screen
a computer screen
a monitor with a 21-inch screen
They were staring at the television screen.
Move your cursor to the top of the screen.
Tessa glanced at the phone's little screen.
an LCD/plasma screen
Hundreds of fans watched on giant television screens.
The image came up on the screen for a few seconds.
The birds appear as red dots on the radar screen.
Information can be viewed on screen or printed out.
the screen display
The system was designed with a menu bar at the bottom of the screen.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the large flat surface that films or pictures are shown on
examples: a cinema/movie screen
an eight-screen cinema
The movie will be coming to your screens shortly.
This film should keep you glued to the screen (= unable to stop watching) for two hours.
The film hits cinema screens in November.
The film demands to be seen on a big screen.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: films or television in general
examples: SEE ALSO big screen
He has adapted the play for the screen.
Some actors never watch themselves on screen.
His face never appears on screen.
She was a star of stage and screen (= plays and films).
a screen actor
She has great screen presence (= she makes a good impression on screen).
He made his screen debut in 1954 as a stable boy.
the screen adaptation (= film) of John Steinbeck's novel East of Eden

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: the data or images shown on a computer screen
examples: SEE ALSO home screen
Press the F1 key to display a help screen.
Can you do a printout of this screen for me?
I posted the screen grab on Twitter.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: a tall, flat piece of furniture or equipment that is fixed to a wall, etc. or that can be moved to divide a room or to keep one area hidden or separate
examples: SEE ALSO fire screen
The nurse put a screen around the bed.
A wooden screen hid one corner of the room.
She went behind the screen and changed into the ballet costume.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: something that prevents somebody from seeing or being aware of something, or that protects somebody/something
examples: SEE ALSO smokescreen
We planted a screen of tall trees.
A screen of bodyguards protected the President.
All the research was conducted behind a screen of secrecy.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: a wire or plastic net that is held in a frame and fastened on a window, or a door, to let in air but keep out insects
examples: Do you have screens on your windows?

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: a wood or stone structure in a church, that partly separates the main area from the altar or choir
examples: SEE ALSO rood screen

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: a system of checking a person or thing to find out whether or not something, typically a disease, is present
examples: You should get a health screen every couple of years.
Candidates for this position must be able to pass a drug screen.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: used to say that people’s attention is on or not on something
examples: The issue of terrorism is back on the radar screen.
Since the scandal broke, all other issues seem to have disappeared off the radar screen as far as the media is concerned.

definitions.label: Meaning 2

definitions.label: Meaning 3

definitions.label: Meaning 4

Airlines often give great deals to fill empty seats.

definitions.label: Meaning 5

definitions.label: Meaning 7

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: the part of the body on which a person sits
examples: SYNONYM bottom (6)

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: the part of a pair of trousers that covers a person’s seat

definitions.label: Meaning 1

examples: COMPARE elementary
secondary teachers
the secondary curriculum

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: less important than something else
examples: That is just a secondary consideration.
Experience is what matters—age is of secondary importance.
Raising animals was only secondary to other forms of farming.
After a while, his writing became secondary to his celebrity.
Forests are secondary in importance only to the oceans in their effects on the earth.
The characters and plot become secondary to the setting and atmosphere.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: happening as a result of something else
examples: a secondary infection
a secondary effect
a secondary colour (= made from mixing two primary colours)
a secondary outcome

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used to introduce the second of a list of points you want to make in a speech or piece of writing
examples: Firstly, it's expensive, and secondly, it's too slow.
First of all, there's no time to do all this, and secondly, it's the wrong thing to be doing anyway.
Secondly, and importantly, cultural influences on behaviour are discussed.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: known about by only a few people; kept hidden from others
examples: SEE ALSO top secret
secret information/meetings/talks
They belong to an age-old secret society.
He tried to keep it secret from his family.
Details of the proposals remain secret.
a secret passage leading to the beach
The two candidates were chosen by a secret ballot (= in which nobody knows how you voted) of MPs.
He's a natural salesman, whose secret weapon is the sheer confidence and optimism that he exudes.
The group is on a highly secret mission.
Secret police documents were leaked to the press.
The scandal was kept secret from the French public for 18 years.
What could be so secret what it had to stay hidden?

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: used to describe actions and behaviour that you do not tell other people about
examples: He's a secret drinker.
I didn't know you were a secret football fan.
her secret fears
Perhaps he has secret hopes that she'll go back to him.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: liking to have secrets that other people do not know about; showing this
examples: SYNONYM secretive
They were so secret about everything.
Jessica caught a secret smile flitting between the two of them.

a legal/medical secretary
the mayor's press secretary

He is secretary to the board of governors.

examples: SEE ALSO general secretary
the membership secretary

secretary to the Jockey Club

definitions.label: Meaning 2

definitions.label: Meaning 3

the sports section of the newspaper

Section by section, this essay examines and explores the key terms.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: a separate group within a larger group of people
examples: SEE ALSO rhythm section
an issue that will affect large sections of the population
the brass section of an orchestra
an area populated largely by the poorer sections of society

We've had meetings with all sections of the community.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: a department in an organization, institution, etc.

definitions.label: Meaning 7

definitions.label: Meaning 3

definitions.label: Meaning 1

definitions.label: Meaning 2

examples: Middle English from Old French seculer, from Latin saecularis, from saeculum ‘generation, age’, used in Christian Latin to mean ‘the world’ (as opposed to the Church).

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to obtain or achieve something, especially when this means using a lot of effort

He secured himself a place at law school.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to attach or fasten something so that it does not move
examples: She secured the rope firmly to the back of the car.

definitions.label: Meaning 15

definitions.label: Meaning 17

They seem to know what they're doing.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: used to make what you say about your thoughts, feelings or actions less strong
examples: I seem to have left my book at home.
I can't seem to (= I've tried, but I can't) get started today.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: used to suggest that something is true when you are not certain or when you want to be polite
examples: It would seem that we all agree.
This last point, it seems to me, is particularly important.
It seems only reasonable to ask students to buy a dictionary.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: in a way that appears to be true but may in fact not be
examples: a seemingly stupid question
a seemingly endless journey
It was a seemingly impossible task.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: according to what you have read or heard
examples: SYNONYM apparently
Seemingly, he borrowed the money from the bank.
They were seemingly having an affair.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a part of something that is separate from the other parts or can be considered separately
examples: She cleaned a small segment of the painting.
Lines divided the area into segments.
The changes will affect only a small segment of the population.
They divided the bone into equal segments.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: one of the sections of an orange, a lemon, etc.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a part of a circle separated from the rest by a single line

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: the smallest speech sound that a word can be divided intoWord Origin
examples: late 16th cent. (as a term in geometry): from Latin segmentum, from secare ‘to cut’. The verb dates from the mid 19th cent.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to take somebody/something in your hand suddenly and using force
examples: SYNONYM grab
She tried to seize the gun from him.
He seized her by the arm.
She seized hold of my hand.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to take control of a place or situation, often suddenly and violently
examples: They seized the airport in a surprise attack.
The army has seized control of the country.
He seized power in a military coup.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to arrest or capture somebody
examples: The men were seized as they left the building.
Terrorists have seized his wife and children.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to take illegal or stolen goods away from somebody
examples: A large quantity of drugs was seized during the raid.
We have the legal right to seize his property.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to be quick to make use of a chance, an opportunity, etc.
examples: SYNONYM grab
The party seized the initiative with both hands (= quickly and with enthusiasm).
She promptly seized the opportunity his absence gave her.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to affect somebody suddenly and deeply
examples: Panic seized her.
He was seized by curiosity.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: if a machine seizes, it no longer works because the parts are stuck and cannot move

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: if a part of your body seizes, you are unable to move it easily and it is often painfulWord Origin
examples: Middle English: from Old French seizir ‘give seisin (possession of land)’, from medieval Latin sacire, in the phrase ad proprium sacire ‘claim as one's own’, from a Germanic base meaning ‘procedure’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: not often
examples: SYNONYM rarely
He had seldom seen a child with so much talent.
She seldom, if ever, goes to the theatre.
They seldom watch television these days.
Seldom had he seen such beauty.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to choose somebody/something from a group of people or things, usually according to a system
examples: He hasn't been selected for the team.
All our hotels have been carefully selected for the excellent value they provide.
She was selected as the parliamentary candidate for Bath.
a randomly selected sample of 23 schools
selected poems of T.S. Eliot
This model is available at selected stores only.
She selected an apple from the fruit bowl.
It is important to select a software package that suits your requirements.
Six theatre companies have been selected to take part in this year's festival.
Select what you want from the options available.
They could select from a range of choices depending on their interests and skills.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to mark something on a computer screen; to choose something, especially from a menu
examples: Select the text you want to format by holding down the left button on your mouse.
Select ‘New Mail’ from the ‘Send’ menu.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the process of choosing somebody/something from a group of people or things, usually according to a system
examples: SEE ALSO self-selection
She took a long time to make her selection.
The final team selection will be made tomorrow.
the random selection of numbers
selection criteria
the selection process
Artists are chosen by a selection committee.
Jury selection in the cases is due to begin next week.
her selection for the England squad
his unexpected selection as party leader

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a number of people or things that have been chosen from a larger group
examples: A selection of readers' comments is published below.
The orchestra played selections from Hollywood musicals.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a collection of things from which something can be chosen
examples: SYNONYM choice
The showroom has a wide selection of kitchens.
The wine selection isn't bad.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: affecting or involving only a small number of people or things from a larger group
examples: the selective breeding of cattle
selective strike action
the socially selective nature of population changes

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: tending to be careful about what or who you choose
examples: You will have to be selective about which information to include in the report.
Their admissions policy is very selective.
a selective school (= one that chooses which children to admit, especially according to ability)

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the type of person you are, especially the way you normally behave, look or feel
examples: You'll soon be feeling your old self again (= feeling well or happy again).
He's not his usual happy self this morning.
Only with a few people could she be her real self (= show what she was really like rather than what she pretended to be).
his private/professional self (= how he behaves at home/work)

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a person’s personality or character that makes them different from other people
examples: Many people living in institutions have lost their sense of self (= the feeling that they are individual people).
the inner self (= a person’s emotional and spiritual character)
a lack of confidence in the self

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: your own advantage or pleasure rather than that of other people
examples: She didn't do it for any reason of self.
Self, self, self! That’s all you ever think about!

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: used to refer to a person
examples: You didn't hurt your little self, did you?
We look forward to seeing Mrs Brown and your good self this evening.
I was very thirsty (note to self: bring water on walks!).

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to not have the strength, influence, etc. that you used to have
examples: When his career ended, he became a shadow of his former self.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to give something to somebody in exchange for money
examples: I recently sold my bike.
His father went bankrupt and the family had to sell their home.
The board agreed to sell the company.
The shares were sold in the open market.
We offered them a good price but they wouldn't sell.
The council is planning to sell the land to developers for housing.
I sold my car to James for £800.
I sold James my car for £800.
They sold the business at a profit/loss (= they gained/lost money when they sold it).
They sold at a loss.
They never buy more than they can sell at a good price.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to offer something for people to buy
examples: COMPARE cross-selling
Most supermarkets sell a range of organic products.
Do you sell stamps?
to sell insurance
His books are sold worldwide.
She decided to sell her work in order to support her family.
They began selling spectacles in 1783.
We sell these little notebooks at €1 each.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to be bought by people in the way or in the numbers mentioned; to be offered at the price mentioned
examples: The book sold well and was reprinted many times.
The new design just didn't sell (= nobody bought it).
The magazine sells 300 000 copies a week.
Their last album sold millions.
The novel was expected to sell between 1 000 and 1 500 copies.
The pens sell for just 50p each.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to make people want to buy something
examples: You may not like it but advertising sells.
It is quality not price that sells our products.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to persuade somebody that something is a good idea, service, product, etc.; to persuade somebody that you are the right person for a job, position, etc.
examples: Now we have to try and sell the idea to management.
You really have to sell yourself at a job interview.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to accept money or a reward from somebody for doing something that is against your principles
examples: SYNONYM prostitute

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to be very enthusiastic about something
examples: We were really sold on the idea.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to be bought quickly or in great numbers

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to have sex with somebody in exchange for money

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: to give poor or unfair treatment to somebody you have promised to help

definitions.label: Meaning 11
definitions.definition: to sell a country's assets, such as land or property, to foreign owners
examples: The government is happy to keep selling off the farm.

definitions.label: Meaning 12
definitions.definition: to sell somebody something/to buy something that has no value or is worth much less than the price paid

definitions.label: Meaning 13
definitions.definition: to not value somebody/yourself highly enough and show this by the way you treat or present them/yourself

definitions.label: Meaning 14
definitions.definition: to do anything, even something really bad or dishonest, in return for money, success or powerWord Origin
examples: Old English sellan (verb), of Germanic origin; related to Old Norse selja ‘give up, sell’. Early use included the sense ‘give, hand (something) over voluntarily following a request’.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a class at a university or college when a small group of students and a teacher discuss or study a particular topic
examples: Teaching is by lectures and seminars.
a graduate seminar
a seminar room

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a meeting for discussion or training
examples: a one-day management seminar

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a member of a senate
examples: Senator McCarthy
She has served as a Democratic senator for North Carolina since 2009.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to make something go or be taken to a place, especially by post, email, radio, etc.
examples: PAST TENSE, PAST PARTICIPLE OF send
She sent a letter of support.
Let me just send this email.
to send something by post
to send something by mail
I sent the package by airmail.
Users were unable to send or receive emails for two days.
Have you sent a Christmas card to your mother yet?
A radio signal was sent to the spacecraft.
Have you sent your mother a Christmas card yet?
I'll send you a text message.
Can you send me a link to the website?
He sent me a copy of his new book.
The laptop was faulty so I sent it back to the manufacturers.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to tell somebody something by sending them a message
examples: My parents send their love.
Henry sent his regards to you.
What sort of message is that sending to young people?
He sent me word to come.
She sent word (that) she could not come.
She sent to say that she was coming home.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to tell somebody to go somewhere or to do something; to arrange for somebody to go somewhere
examples: Ed couldn't make it so they sent me instead.
She sent the kids to bed early.
The judge sent her to prison for two years.
He was sent away to boarding school at the age of eight.
The government has agreed to send 3 000 troops to the region.
We are being sent on a training course next month.
Children were sent home from school because it was just too hot.
I've sent Tom to buy some milk.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to make something/somebody move quickly or suddenly
examples: Every step he took sent the pain shooting up his leg.
The punch sent him flying.
The report sent share prices down a further 8p.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to make somebody behave or react in a particular way
examples: Her music always sends me to sleep.
Her account of the visit sent us into fits of laughter.
All the publicity nearly sent him crazy.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to tell somebody clearly or rudely to go away
examples: She tried to interfere but I sent her packing.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: used to say that you should accept an unpleasant situation or event because you cannot change itWord Origin
examples: Old English sendan, of Germanic origin; related to Dutch zenden and German senden.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: high in rank or status; higher in rank or status than others
examples: OPPOSITE junior
a senior official/officer/manager/executive
a senior adviser/analyst/lecturer
a senior partner in a law firm
She is senior vice president of marketing.
senior figures in the Labour party
senior members of staff
a senior position
a senior post/job
I have ten years' experience at senior management level.
Junior nurses usually work alongside more senior nurses.
He is a former senior civil servant who now runs a campaign website.
He is senior to me.
The meeting should be chaired by the most senior person present.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: for adults or people at a more advanced level
examples: to take part in senior competitions
his first game of senior football
He won the senior men's 400 metres.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: for senior citizens (= older people, especially those who have retired from work)
examples: Get one third off rail fares with a senior railcard.
senior discounts/concessions

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: used after the name of a man who has the same name as his son, to make it clear who is being referred to
examples: COMPARE junior

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: for children over the age of 11 or 13

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: connected with the last year in high school or college
examples: the senior prom

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a feeling that you get when something affects your body
examples: a tingling/burning sensation
I had a sensation of falling, as if in a dream.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the ability to feel through your sense of touch
examples: SYNONYM feeling
She seemed to have lost all sensation in her arms.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a general feeling or impression that is difficult to explain; an experience or a memory
examples: He had the eerie sensation of being watched.
When I arrived, I had the sensation that she had been expecting me.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: very great surprise, excitement, or interest among a lot of people; the person or the thing that causes this surprise
examples: News of his arrest caused a sensation.
The band became a sensation overnight.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: an understanding about something; an ability to judge something
examples: SEE ALSO road sense
One of the most important things in a partner is a sense of humour (= the ability to find things funny or make people laugh).
He has a very good sense of direction (= finds the way to a place easily).
She has lost all sense of direction in her life (= the idea of what she should do in her life).
Always try to keep a sense of proportion (= of the relative importance of different things).
a sense of rhythm/timing
a sense of fun/adventure
Readers gain a real sense of what life was like in the camp.
Alex doesn't have any dress sense (= does not know which clothes look attractive).

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: good understanding and judgement; knowledge of what is sensible or practical behaviour
examples: SEE ALSO common sense
You should have the sense to take advice when it is offered.
There's no sense in (= it is not sensible) worrying about it now.
Can't you talk sense (= say something sensible)?
There's a lot of sense in what Mary says.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: the meaning that a word or phrase has; a way of understanding something
examples: That word has three senses.
The word ‘love’ is used in different senses by different people.
Globalization in the broadest sense is nothing new.
The word ‘perspective’ is being used here in a technical sense.
He was a true friend, in every sense of the word (= in every possible way).
In a sense (= in one way) it doesn't matter any more.
In some senses (= in one or more ways) the criticisms were justified.
In no sense can the issue be said to be resolved.
I am using ‘cold’ in the sense of ‘unfriendly’.
I don't mean that the press ought to be free in the sense that no one ought to pay for it.
There is a sense in which we are all to blame for the tragedy.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: one of the five powers (sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch) that your body uses to get information about the world around you
examples: SEE ALSO sixth sense
the five senses
Dogs have a keen sense (= strong sense) of smell.
the sense organs (= eyes, ears, nose, etc.)
I could hardly believe the evidence of my own senses (= what I could see, hear, etc.).
The mixture of sights, smells and sounds around her made her senses reel.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: a feeling about something important
examples: His career was guided by a strong sense of duty.
There is now a sense of urgency to fix the problem.
I have found a sense of purpose in the work I do here.
Most people in the country have a strong sense of national identity.
My parents instilled a strong sense of responsibility in me.
Clubs try to create a sense of community.
Helmets can give cyclists a false sense of security.
He felt an overwhelming sense of loss.
I had the sense that he was worried about something.
I got the sense that she wasn't very pleased to see us.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: a normal state of mind; the ability to think clearly
examples: If she threatens to leave, it should bring him to his senses.
He waited for Dora to come to her senses and return.
No one in their right senses would give him the job!
Are you out of your senses? You'll be killed!

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to try and persuade somebody to stop behaving in a stupid way, sometimes using rough or violent methods
examples: Try and talk some sense into her before she makes the wrong decision.
Where would I be without you to knock some sense into my head?

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to have a meaning that you can easily understand
examples: This sentence doesn't make sense.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to be a sensible thing to do
examples: It makes sense to buy the most up-to-date version.
There are strict medicals for pilots, which makes good sense.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: to be easy to understand or explain
examples: John wasn't making much sense on the phone.
Who would send me all these flowers? It makes no sense.
It all made perfect sense to me.

definitions.label: Meaning 11
definitions.definition: to understand something that is difficult or has no clear meaning
examples: I can’t make sense of that painting.

definitions.label: Meaning 12
definitions.definition: to start to be sensible or reasonable
examples: I tried to make him see sense, but he just wouldn't listen.

definitions.label: Meaning 13
definitions.definition: a feeling or understanding that an event is important or special
examples: Candles on the table gave the evening a sense of occasion.

definitions.label: Meaning 14
definitions.definition: to start behaving as if you are crazyWord Origin
examples: late Middle English (as a noun in the sense ‘meaning’): from Latin sensus ‘faculty of feeling, thought, meaning’, from sentire ‘feel’. The verb dates from the mid 16th cent.

definitions.definition: able to make good judgements based on reason and experience rather than emotion; practical

We are just asking people to be sensible about the amount of water they use.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: useful rather than fashionable
examples: sensible shoes

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: aware of something
examples: OPPOSITE insensible

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: aware of and able to understand other people and their feelings
examples: OPPOSITE insensitive
a sensitive and caring man
She is very sensitive to other people's feelings.

examples: OPPOSITE insensitive
sensitive areas of the body

The eyes of some fish are acutely sensitive to light.

These drugs can make skin extremely sensitive to sunlight.
Coral reefs are very sensitive to changes in seawater temperature.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: able to understand art, music and literature and to express yourself through them
examples: an actor’s sensitive reading of the poem
a sensitive portrait

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: easily offended or upset
examples: OPPOSITE insensitive

He's very sensitive about his weight.
She's very sensitive to criticism.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: that you have to treat with great care because it may offend people or make them angry or embarrassed

highly sensitive documents

definitions.definition: a set of words expressing a statement, a question or an order, usually containing a subject and a verb. In written English sentences begin with a capital letter and end with a full stop/period (.), a question mark (?) or an exclamation mark (!).

There are mistakes in grammar, sentence structure and punctuation.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to prepare or arrange something so that it is ready for use or in position
examples: Have you set the alarm clock?

I set my watch by (= make it show the same time as) the TV.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to arrange knives, forks, etc. on a table for a meal
examples: Can you help me set the table?
Could you set the table for dinner?

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to fix something so that others copy it or try to achieve it
examples: This could set a new fashion.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to give somebody a piece of work to do or a task or target to achieve

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to be located in a particular place
examples: The house is set in fifty acres of parkland.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to put something/somebody in a particular place or position
examples: She set a tray down on the table.

definitions.definition: to cause somebody/something to be in a particular state; to start something happening

definitions.label: Meaning 10

definitions.label: Meaning 11

definitions.label: Meaning 12

definitions.label: Meaning 13

definitions.label: Meaning 14

definitions.label: Meaning 15

definitions.label: Meaning 1

definitions.label: Meaning 2

definitions.label: Meaning 3

definitions.label: Meaning 4

definitions.label: Meaning 5

definitions.label: Meaning 6

definitions.label: Meaning 7

definitions.label: Meaning 8

definitions.label: Meaning 2

definitions.label: Meaning 3

definitions.label: Meaning 4

definitions.label: Meaning 6

definitions.label: Meaning 7

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to put an end to an argument or a disagreement

to settle a case/lawsuit/claim
to settle an argument/a disagreement

There is pressure on the unions to settle.
The company has agreed to settle out of court (= come to an agreement without going to court).

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to decide or arrange something finally
examples: It's all settled—we're leaving on the nine o'clock plane.
Good, that's settled, then.
Bob will be there? That settles it. I'm not coming.
He had to settle his affairs (= arrange all his personal business) in Paris before he could return home.
It's been settled that we leave on the nine o'clock plane.
All the loose ends should be settled within 48 hours.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to make a place your permanent home
examples: She settled in Vienna after her father's death.

He has now settled permanently in London.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to make your permanent home in a country or an area as colonists

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to make yourself or somebody else comfortable in a new position
examples: Ellie settled back in her seat.

I settled her on the sofa and put a blanket over her.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to put something carefully in a position so that it does not move
examples: She settled the blanket around her knees.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to become or make somebody/something become calm or relaxed
examples: The baby wouldn't settle.

This should settle your stomach.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to fall from above and come to rest on something; to stay for some time on something
examples: Dust had settled on everything.
Two birds settled on the fence.
I don't think the snow will settle (= remain on the ground without melting).
His gaze settled on her face.
Slowly dusk began to settle.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to sink slowly down; to make something do this
examples: The contents of the package may have settled in transit.

definitions.label: Meaning 10

The insurance company is refusing to settle her claim.
They used the last of the money to settle their debts.
Let me settle with you for the meal.
I'll pay now—we can settle up later.

definitions.label: Meaning 11

examples: He waited for the dust to settle after the election before making any new decisions.

definitions.label: Meaning 12

definitions.label: Meaning 2

definitions.label: Meaning 3

signs of an Iron Age settlement
a mining settlement

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: an area that is dark and cool under or behind something, for example a tree or building, because the sun’s light does not get to it
examples: SEE ALSO shady

The temperature can reach 40°C in the shade.
We sat down in the shade of the wall.
These plants grow well in sun or shade.
Two cows were sleeping under the shade of some trees.
The trees provide shade for the animals in the summer.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a thing that you use to prevent light from coming through or to make it less bright
examples: SEE ALSO lampshade
I bought a new shade for the lamp.
an eyeshade

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: material that covers a window, often consisting of a roll of cloth that is fixed at the top of the window and can be pulled up and down

definitions.label: Meaning 4

examples: a dark/light/pale/bright shade of blue
a subtle/delicate shade of grey
His face turned an even deeper shade of red.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: the dark areas in a picture, especially the use of these to produce variety
examples: The painting needs more light and shade.

examples: politicians of all shades of opinion

reformers of all political shades

definitions.label: Meaning 7

examples: SYNONYM touch

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: sunglasses (= a pair of glasses with dark glass in them that you wear to protect your eyes from bright light from the sun)

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: the spirit of a dead person; a ghost

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: to be much better or more impressive than somebody/something
examples: I tried hard but her work put mine in the shade.

definitions.label: Meaning 11
definitions.definition: used when you are referring to things that remind you of a particular person, thing or time
examples: short skirts and long boots—shades of the 1960s

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the dark shape that somebody/something’s form makes on a surface, for example on the ground, when they are between the light and the surface
examples: SEE ALSO 5 o'clock shadow
The children were having fun, chasing each other's shadows.
As the curtains moved in the breeze, the shadows on the floor seemed to dance.
The ship's sail cast a shadow on the water.
The shadows lengthened as the sun went down.
The man's face is hidden in a deep shadow cast by his umbrella.
They saw the shadow of a man pass by.
He didn't want to cast a shadow on (= spoil) their happiness.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: darkness in a place or on something, especially so that you cannot easily see who or what is there
examples: I thought I saw a figure standing in the shadows.
His face was deep in shadow, turned away from her.
A man in black emerged from the shadows.
It had grown dark, and the shadows could be hiding anything.
It's a spooky story about the monsters that lurk in the shadows.
She shrank back into the shadows as the footsteps approached.
‘I'm right here,’ I said, stepping out of the shadows.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: a very small amount of something
examples: SYNONYM hint

She knew beyond a shadow of a doubt (= with no doubt at all) that he was lying.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: the strong (often bad) influence of somebody/something
examples: The new leader wants to escape from the shadow of his predecessor.
Bergman casts a long shadow over world cinema.
These people have been living for years under the shadow of fear.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: dark areas under somebody’s eyes, because they are tired, etc.
examples: She looked pale, with deep shadows under her eyes.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: a person or an animal that follows somebody else all the time

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: a thing that is not real or possible to obtain
examples: You can't spend all your life chasing shadows.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to be very easily frightened; to be very nervous

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to not have the strength, influence, etc. that you used to have
examples: When his career ended, he became a shadow of his former self.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: very close to
examples: The new market is in the shadow of the City Hall.

definitions.label: Meaning 11
definitions.definition: when you say that somebody is in/under the shadow of another person, you mean that they do not receive as much attention as that person
examples: A younger son often lives in the shadow of his elder brother.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to move or make somebody/something move with short quick movements from side to side or up and down
examples: The whole house shakes when a train goes past.
Shake the bottle well before use.
The explosion shook windows miles from the site.
He shook her violently by the shoulders.
He knelt and gently shook her awake.
She shook her hair loose.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to move something in a particular direction by shaking
examples: She bent down to shake a pebble out of her shoe.
His father used to come home and shake the dust off his work clothes.
He stood up, shaking sand everywhere.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to take somebody’s hand and move it up and down as a way of saying hello or to show that you agree about something
examples: Do people in Italy shake hands when they meet?
She refused to shake hands with him.
He stepped forward and shook my hand.
Our host shook each of us warmly by the hand.
They shook hands on the deal (= to show that they had reached an agreement).
They shook on the deal (= shook hands to show the deal was agreed).
Let's shake on it.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to turn your head from side to side as a way of saying ‘no’ or to show that you are sad, feel doubt, etc.
examples: ‘Drink?’ he offered. She shook her head.
The old man watched them walk off into the night, shaking his head sadly.
She shook her head in disbelief.
He shook his head at the thought.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to show that you are angry with somebody; to threaten somebody by shaking your fist (= closed hand)
examples: The man shook his fist at the court after he was sentenced.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to make short quick movements that you cannot control, for example because you are cold or afraid
examples: SYNONYM tremble
Her hands had started to shake.
He was shaking with fear.
He saw his mother turn away, her shoulders shaking with laughter.
His whole body shook with rage.
I was shaking like a leaf.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to sound unsteady, usually because you are nervous, upset or angry
examples: ‘Who are you?’ he asked, his voice shaking.
Her voice shook with emotion.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to shock or upset somebody very much
examples: He was badly shaken by the news of her death.
The accident really shook her up.
Shaken up by the early goal against them, the team began to fight back.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to make a belief or an idea less certain
examples: The incident had shaken her faith in him.
This announcement is bound to shake the confidence of the industry.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: to get rid of something
examples: I can't seem to shake off this cold.
She has finally managed to shake off her old wrist injury.
He couldn't shake the feeling that there was something wrong.
She never seemed to completely shake off the dumb blonde image.

definitions.label: Meaning 11
definitions.definition: to cause people to question their basic beliefs about something
examples: This issue has shaken the foundations of French politics.
an event which rocked the foundations of British politics

definitions.label: Meaning 12
definitions.definition: to be very frightened or nervous

definitions.definition: used to show that you are determined, or to give an order or instruction
examples: He is determined that you shall succeed.
Candidates shall remain in their seats until all the papers have been collected.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: not having much distance between the top or surface and the bottom
examples: OPPOSITE deep
a shallow dish/pan/bowl
a shallow sea/lake/pool/pond
They were playing in the shallow end (= of the swimming pool).
These fish are found in shallow waters around the coast.
The body was found in a shallow grave.
Most earthquakes occur at much shallower depths.
shallow roots (= that grow near the surface of the ground)

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: not showing serious thought, feelings, etc. about something
examples: SYNONYM superficial
This shows how shallow their commitment to the environment really is.
Tony seemed very shallow and immature.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: shallow breathing involves taking in only a small amount of air each timeWord Origin
examples: late Middle English: obscurely related to shoal sense (2).

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: used to say that something is a cause for feeling sad or disappointed
examples: SYNONYM pity
She's retiring because of ill health, which is a great shame.
What happened was a real shame.
It's a shame that she wasn't here to see it.
Shame they didn't think of that earlier.
It’s a shame (that) you didn’t say something sooner.
What a shame they couldn't come.
It's a shame about Tim, isn't it?
It's a terrible shame about Stuart losing his job, isn't it?
It's a shame to see her wasting her talent like this.
It'd be a shame for us to give up now.
It would be a crying shame (= a great shame) not to take them up on the offer.
It seems such a shame to throw perfectly good food away.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: the feelings of being sad, embarrassed or guilty that you have when you know that something you have done is wrong or stupid
examples: His face burned with shame.
They should blush with shame.
She hung her head in shame.
The king preferred death to the shame of defeat.
It took me a while to get over the shame of not doing something to help him.
He could not live with the shame of other people knowing the truth.
I felt a twinge of shame at the thought.
She admitted her shame at having a parent in prison.
He was filled with shame for giving in to his anger.
She expressed her shame for her role in the whole unfortunate business.
I would die of shame if she ever found out.
To my shame (= I feel shame that) I refused to listen to her side of the story.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: the ability to feel shame at something you have done
examples: Have you no shame?
That child is completely without shame!
She has no sense of shame.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: the loss of respect that is caused when you do something wrong or stupid
examples: There is no shame in wanting to be successful.
She felt that her failure would bring shame on her family.
He risked public shame and possible imprisonment.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to be much better than somebody/something
examples: Their presentation put ours to shame.
Her energy and enthusiasm puts the rest of us to shame (= makes us feel embarrassed and guilty that we are not the same).

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: used to say that somebody should feel ashamed for something they have said or done
examples: Shame on you for doubting me!

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: the form of the outer edges or surfaces of something; an example of something that has a particular form
examples: a rectangular/spherical/cylindrical shape
geometric shapes
fantastic creatures that can change shape and be either visible or invisible
You can recognize the fish by the shape of their fins.
They have completely different body shapes.
This old T-shirt has completely lost its shape.
The island was originally circular in shape.
Several rooms are irregular in shape.
Candles come in all shapes and sizes.
Glass is blown or moulded into many shapes.
The pool was in the shape of a heart.
The government provides money in the shape of (= consisting of) grants and student loans.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: a person or thing that is difficult to see clearly
examples: SYNONYM figure
Ghostly shapes moved around in the dark.
I could just make out a dark shape in the distance.
An enormous shape loomed up out of the mist directly in front of me.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: the physical condition of somebody/something
examples: What sort of shape was the car in after the accident?
He's in good shape for a man of his age.
The ship was in bad shape as a result of damage sustained in the collision.
He’s not in any shape (= not well enough) to be working.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: the particular qualities or characteristics of something
examples: Will new technology change the shape of broadcasting?
Prices vary according to the size and shape of each project.
He did much to determine the shape of Asia's political map.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to become angry, anxious or upset
examples: Don't get bent out of shape about it. It was just a mistake!

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to take exercise, eat healthy food, etc. in order to become physically fit
examples: I’m trying to get into shape before summer.
I need to get back into shape after the Christmas holiday.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to train somebody so that they do a particular job, task, etc. well
examples: It took him just two weeks to knock the new recruits into shape.
Leave the boy with me—I'll soon knock him into shape!

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to make something more acceptable, organized or successful
examples: I've got all the information together but it still needs knocking into shape.
It shouldn’t take long to get the company back into shape.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to express or explain a particular idea, plan, etc.
examples: Marie tried to find the right words to give shape to the confusion in her head.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: of any type
examples: I don't approve of violence in any shape or form.
I can't stand insects in any shape or form.
I do not condone bullying in any way, shape or form.

definitions.label: Meaning 11
definitions.definition: (to get/stay) in good physical condition
examples: You don't have to spend a fortune on gym membership to get in shape.
I like to stay in shape.

definitions.label: Meaning 12
definitions.definition: not having the normal shape
examples: The wheel had been twisted out of shape.
The bicycle had been battered out of shape.

definitions.label: Meaning 13
definitions.definition: not in good physical condition
examples: I didn’t realize how out of shape I was!

definitions.label: Meaning 14
definitions.definition: the way things are likely to develop in the future
examples: Are solar-powered cars the shape of things to come?
This new system could be the shape of things to come.

definitions.label: Meaning 15
definitions.definition: to develop and become more complete or organized
examples: The garden is beginning to take shape.
A new song began to take shape in her mind.

definitions.label: Meaning 16
definitions.definition: to dance
examples: She spent the whole evening throwing shapes on the dance floor.

definitions.label: Meaning 17
definitions.definition: to behave in a way that makes you seem to threaten somebody, especially by standing as though you are ready to fight, without actually becoming violent
examples: I was worried he might get violent but he was just throwing shapes.
The two main investors threw some shapes during the debate.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: having the type of shape mentioned
examples: SEE ALSO pear-shaped
a huge balloon shaped like a giant cow
almond-shaped eyes
an L-shaped room

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to have, use or experience something at the same time as somebody else
examples: There isn't an empty table. Would you mind sharing?
to share a room/bed
Parents said there was insufficient room for the two schools to share space.
It's been 23 years since these four men shared a stage.
Sue shares a house with three other students.
Bob told Jess he wanted to share his life with her.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to have part of something while another person or other people also have part
examples: All members of the band equally share the band's profits.
He shared the pie with her.
The Hungarian king shared power with the Austrian emperor to form the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
Each partner is entitled to share in the profits of the business.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to divide something between two or more people
examples: SEE ALSO job-sharing
We shared the pizza between the four of us.
Rita shared her money out among her six grandchildren.
Profits are shared out yearly.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: to give some of what you have to somebody else; to let somebody use something that is yours
examples: John had no brothers or sisters and wasn't used to sharing.
The conference is a good place to share information and exchange ideas.
This online resource will give farmers a new way to share knowledge with each other.
Eli shared his chocolate with the other kids.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to have the same feelings, ideas, experiences, etc. as somebody else
examples: to share a concern/an opinion
shared values
They shared a common interest in botany.
a view that is widely shared
They share a love of cinema.
His son doesn't share his passion for athletics.
Sikhs share this belief with followers of other Indian religions.
People often share their political views with their parents.
I didn't really share in her love of animals.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to tell other people about your ideas, experiences, and feelings
examples: to share thoughts/ideas/feelings/memories
Men often don't like to share their problems.
The two friends shared everything—they had no secrets.
Please share this on Facebook and Twitter so we can get the word out.
I want to share the stories of several people I met.
Think of this as an opportunity to share your experiences.
The group listens while one person shares (= tells other people about their experiences, feelings, etc.).
Would you like to share your experience with the rest of the group?

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to be equally involved in something or responsible for something
examples: Both drivers shared the blame for the accident.
Don't try to do everything yourself: you will need to share the load with your partner.
Responsibility is shared between parents and teachers.
I try to get the kids to share in the housework.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: used to say that everyone should share things equally and in a fair way

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: if you talk to somebody about your problems and worries, instead of keeping them to yourself, they seem less seriousWord Origin
examples: verb Old English scearu ‘division, part into which something may be divided’, of Germanic origin; related to Dutch schare and German Schar ‘troop, multitude’, also to shear. The verb dates from the late 16th cent.

examples: the major shareholders in the company
Company shareholders approved the merger.
He has attracted new and existing shareholders to invest in his company.
He was voicing the concerns of ordinary shareholders.
The government is still a majority shareholder in the industry.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: having a fine edge or point, especially of something that can cut or make a hole in something
examples: OPPOSITE blunt
a sharp knife
Toys with sharp edges are not suitable for young children.
sharp teeth
Take a sheet of paper and a sharp pencil.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: sudden and rapid, especially of a change in something
examples: a sharp drop in prices
a sharp rise in crime
a sharp increase in unemployment
the sharp decline in the value of the pound against the dollar
He heard a sharp intake of breath.
We need to give young criminals a short, sharp shock (= a punishment that is very unpleasant for a short time).

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: clear and definite
examples: a sharp outline

She drew a sharp distinction between domestic and international politics.
In sharp contrast to her mood, the clouds were breaking up to reveal a blue sky.
The issue must be brought into sharper focus.
The image looks very sharp and nicely detailed.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: quick to notice or understand things or to react
examples: to have sharp eyes
a girl of sharp intelligence
a sharp sense of humour
He kept a sharp lookout for any strangers.
It was very sharp of you to see that!
Her mind was as sharp as a razor.

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: critical or severe
examples: sharp criticism
Emma has a sharp tongue (= she often speaks in an unpleasant or unkind way).
He was very sharp with me when I was late.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: loud, sudden and often high in tone
examples: She read out the list in sharp, clipped tones.
There was a sharp knock on the door.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: very strong and sudden, often like being cut or badly hurt
examples: SYNONYM intense
He winced as a sharp pain shot through his leg.
Polly felt a sharp pang of jealousy.

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: changing direction suddenly
examples: a sharp bend in the road
a sharp turn to the left

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: strong and slightly bitter
examples: The cheese has a distinctively sharp taste.

definitions.label: Meaning 10
definitions.definition: used to describe a very cold or very severe frost or wind
examples: SEE ALSO razor-sharp

definitions.label: Meaning 11
definitions.definition: clever but possibly dishonest
examples: His lawyer's a sharp operator.
The firm had to face some sharp practice from competing companies.

definitions.label: Meaning 12
definitions.definition: fashionable and new
examples: The consultants were a group of men in sharp suits.
Todd is a sharp dresser.

definitions.label: Meaning 13
definitions.definition: not full or round in shape
examples: a man with a thin face and sharp features (= a pointed nose and chin)

definitions.label: Meaning 14
definitions.definition: used after the name of a note to mean a note a semitone higher
examples: OPPOSITE flat
the Piano Sonata in C sharp minor

definitions.label: Meaning 15
definitions.definition: above the correct pitch (= how high or low a note sounds)
examples: OPPOSITE flat
That note sounded sharp.

definitions.label: Meaning 16
definitions.definition: not intelligent
examples: He's not exactly the sharpest knife in the drawer, is he?

definitions.label: Meaning 17
definitions.definition: the place or position of greatest difficulty or responsibility
examples: He started work at the sharp end of the business, as a salesman.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to suddenly break into small pieces; to make something suddenly break into small pieces
examples: He dropped the vase and it shattered into pieces on the floor.
The mirror shattered into a thousand pieces.
the sound of shattering glass
The explosion shattered all the windows in the building.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to destroy something completely, especially somebody’s feelings, hopes or beliefs; to be destroyed in this way
examples: Anna's self-confidence had been completely shattered.
Injury shattered his dreams of competing in the Olympics.
Her experience of divorce shattered her illusions about love.
My whole world shattered into a million pieces.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to make somebody feel extremely shocked and upset
examples: The unexpected death of their son shattered them.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: a female person or animal that has already been mentioned or is easily identified
examples: COMPARE her
‘What does your sister do?’ ‘She's a dentist.’
Doesn't she (= the woman we are looking at) look like Sue?
Think about a friend or family member. What kind of person is he or she?

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: it (used to refer to something not usually thought of as female)
examples: She's a big country.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: to get rid of something that is no longer wanted
examples: The factory is shedding a large number of jobs.
a quick way to shed unwanted pounds (= extra weight or fat on your body)
Museums have been trying hard to shed their stuffy image.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to take off a piece of clothing
examples: We shed our jackets.
Luke shed his clothes onto the floor.

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: to lose or drop what it is carrying
examples: The traffic jam was caused by a lorry shedding its load.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: if an animal sheds its skin, or a plant sheds leaves, it loses them naturally
examples: How often does a snake shed its skin?
trees that shed their leaves in autumn

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to send light over something; to let light fall somewhere
examples: The candles shed a soft glow on her face.

definitions.label: Meaning 6
definitions.definition: to cry
examples: She shed no tears when she heard he was dead.

definitions.label: Meaning 7
definitions.definition: to kill or injure people, especially in a war
examples: SEE ALSO bloodshed
How much blood will be shed before the fighting ends?

definitions.label: Meaning 8
definitions.definition: to have the quality of causing water or liquid to run off and not sink in
examples: A duck's feathers shed water immediately.

definitions.label: Meaning 9
definitions.definition: to make a problem, etc. easier to understand
examples: Recent research has shed new light on the causes of the disease.

definitions.label: Meaning 1
definitions.definition: an animal with a thick coat, kept on farms for its meat (called mutton or lamb) or its wool
examples: COMPARE ewe
a flock of sheep
Sheep were grazing in the fields.
sheep farmers
These leaves are toxic to cattle and sheep.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: to imagine that sheep are jumping over a fence and to count them, as a way of getting to sleep

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: if people behave like sheep, they all do what the others are doing, without thinking for themselves

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: if you are going to be punished for doing something wrong, whether it is a big or small thing, you may as well do the big thing

definitions.label: Meaning 5
definitions.definition: to recognize the difference between people who are good at something, intelligent, etc. and those who are not

definitions.label: Meaning 6

definitions.label: Meaning 1

examples: The area is under threat from the sheer number of tourists using it.
We were impressed by the sheer size of the cathedral.

definitions.label: Meaning 2
definitions.definition: complete and not mixed with anything else
examples: SYNONYM utter

sheer luck/chance/coincidence/joy/bliss/determination
I only agreed out of sheer desperation.
sheer terror/panic/exhaustion/hell

definitions.label: Meaning 3
definitions.definition: very steep
examples: sheer cliffs/slopes
Outside there was a sheer drop down to the sea below.

definitions.label: Meaning 4
definitions.definition: thin, light and almost transparent
examples: sheer nylon

definitions.label: Meaning 1
